author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: In a certain town, which for reasons of prudence shall remain nameless, there stood a building of profound public utility: the parish workhouse. Within these bleak, whitewashed walls, upon a day and year of little consequence to anyone but the parish overseers, was born the item of mortality whose name is prefixed to the head of this chapter. For a considerable duration following his initial introduction to this sorrowful world, it remained a matter of considerable doubt whether the fragile infant would draw breath enough to claim a name at all. Had he expired then, his biography would have possessed the rare and inestimable virtue of being incredibly brief, and entirely, flawlessly true.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: The wretched little creature gasped and struggled for that troublesome commodity, air, upon a flock bed of questionable cleanliness. Providence, in its infinite mercy, had spared him the presence of profound medical men and weeping, anxious aunts; leaving him solely to the tender mercies of a pauper nurse, steeped in gin, and Nature herself. Unhindered by medical science, he eventually sneezed, drew a long, shuddering breath, and announced his arrival with a cry that echoed through the damp and dreary ward.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: With a sudden, sharp cry that pierced the gloom of the parish ward, the infant announced his arrival; a sound which fluttered the tattered blankets of a nearby iron bedstead. A pale and exhausted young woman, hitherto lying as one dead, stirred at the noise. With a desperate, trembling effort, she raised her head from the thin pillow and, in a voice scarcely louder than a sigh, pleaded to behold the child before her own life ebbed entirely away.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: The medical gentleman, with an air of profound indifference, deposited the squalling bundle of humanity into the mother's weak arms. She pressed her cold, white lips to the infant’s forehead in a final, desperate kiss of maternal love, shuddered violently, and fell back into the eternal sleep. The parish surgeon leaned over the lifeless clay, felt for a pulse that was no longer there, and casually announced the departure of her soul, as if he were remarking upon the weather.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: “It’s all over, Mrs. Thingummy!” declared the medical gentleman, casually adjusting his spectacles as he gazed upon the lifeless clay. The nurse, whose attentions were far less fixed upon the departed soul than upon a certain green glass bottle she had hastily concealed within the folds of her garments, offered a swift and mechanical murmur of sympathetic agreement, wiping a dry eye with the corner of her filthy apron.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: “Ah, poor dear, so it is!” echoed the misty-eyed nurse, a creature of profound parish experience and undeniable intoxication. She arranged her features into a mask of professional mourning, though her mind was entirely occupied with the prospect of returning to her hidden liquid consolations the very instant the medical gentleman’s back was turned.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: “If the troublesome little brat cries, give it some gruel,” instructed the surgeon, drawing on his gloves with a snap of finality. He paused at the door, casting a cold, appraising eye back at the bed. “A remarkably good-looking girl, that. One wonders what gutter she crawled out of, or what particular path of ruin led her to our hospitable doors.”

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: “The overseer brought her in last night,” croaked the old woman, leaning heavily against the bedpost. “Found her dying in the street, she was. Her shoes were worn to dust, torn and bleeding her feet were, showing she’d walked a terrible long way. But from whence she came, or whither she was bound when she fell, only God Almighty knows.”

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: Lifting the cold, lifeless left hand, the surgeon shook his head with a cynical, knowing smile. “The old story,” he muttered, dropping the limb back onto the bed. “No wedding-ring. A familiar tragedy in this grand and glorious country of ours! Well, good night to you!” And with that, he marched out of the room.

author: Charles Dickens
ai_styled_text: Thus the medical gentleman departed to the comforts of his warm dinner; whilst the nurse, fortifying her nerves with another robust and lengthy draft from the green bottle, sat down upon a low stool before the dying fire.
